title: Engineering correlated phases through manipulation of Van Hove singularities
authors: Thomas P. Sheerin, Maria Ramirez, Chris A. Hooley, Luke C. Rhodes
abstract: Controlling the ordered phases of correlated electron systems remains a central challenge in quantum materials design. Divergences in the electronic density of states, known as Van Hove singularities (VHSs), are one obvious route to such control. It is clear from recent work that the exact functional form of these divergences can profoundly affect which phases are realized; a full picture, however, remains elusive. In this work, we use both the hot-spot parquet renormalization group and the truncated-unity functional renormalization group to theoretically study the emergent correlated states of a two-dimensional square-lattice Hubbard model with VHSs at or near the Fermi level. By varying a single hopping parameter, $t_3$, we are able to change the strength of the VHS divergence in the density of states from logarithmic (for $t_3 < t_{3c}$) to power-law (for $t_3 = t_{3c}$). Further increase of $t_3$ ($t_3 > t_{3c}$) causes each original Van Hove point to split into two, both of the conventional logarithmic type. We show that which of these regimes we are in strongly influences the predicted ordered states. We also study the dependence on doping, and find that the ferromagnetic state that occurs at Van Hove filling in these models is unstable to very small shifts in the Fermi level, often giving way to distinct ordered states depending on whether the model is electron- or hole-doped. These results highlight the importance of tuning VHS properties to control ordered states in correlated materials, and offer design rules to engineer these phases in novel systems.
summary: This work theoretically investigates how tuning Van Hove singularities in a 2D Hubbard model controls the ordered phases of correlated electrons. By varying hopping parameters, the researchers change the nature of the electronic density of states from logarithmic to power-law divergences. The results demonstrate that these VHS properties are crucial design rules for engineering specific quantum ground states.
main_problem: The central challenge is controlling the ordered phases of correlated electron systems by manipulating Van Hove singularities (VHSs) in their electronic structure.
main_result: The type and strength of VHS divergences—which can be tuned from logarithmic to power-law via hopping parameters—strongly dictate the predicted ground state, leading to distinct ordered phases depending on doping.
method: Theoretical analysis using advanced renormalization group techniques, specifically the hot-spot parquet (pRG) and truncated-unity functional renormalization group (TUFRG).
model_or_system: The study focuses on a two-dimensional square-lattice Hubbard model characterized by hopping parameters ($t_1, t_2, t_3$) that allow tuning the nature of VHSs at or near the Fermi level.
key_observables: Predicted ordered states (e.g., ferromagnetic, superconducting, SDW), and the flow behavior of coupling constants derived from susceptibilities ($\Pi^q_{	ext{ph}}, \Pi^q_{	ext{pp}}$).
important_parameters: The third-neighbor hopping parameter ($t_3$), which controls the VHS divergence type (logarithmic, power-law, or split), and doping level relative to Van Hove filling.
main_assumptions: The pRG relies on a 'hot-spot approximation,' while TUFRG is presented as a more comprehensive alternative for studying the low-energy physics near singularities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the non-interacting Fermi surfaces and Density of States (DOS) across three regimes defined by $t_3$: single-VHS, HOVHS, and split-VHS. Later figures map out phase diagrams showing SDW wavevectors $(\delta, \delta)$ as a function of doping and interaction strength.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the low-energy physics by first establishing the model and the parameter space defined by $t_3$. It then applies pRG/TUFRG to derive flow equations for coupling constants in each VHS regime, culminating in phase diagram analysis showing how doping shifts the system between different ordered states.
why_interesting: The explicit connection drawn between a tunable band structure feature (VHS divergence type) and the resulting emergent quantum ground state is highly relevant for designing novel correlated materials.
